as_of_utc: 2026-09-14 (exact UTC time not captured by tools; session date confirmed as 2026-09-14)

facts.fact: KIUC had restored power to more than 80% of its members, the most recent figure available
About 8,400 KIUC members remained without power, most on the North Shore between Moloaa and Haena, with scattered pockets from Anahola to Kekaha and Kokee
76% of KIUC members had power restored as of Saturday
At the storm's peak, roughly 90% of KIUC accounts (33,000 of 36,000) lost power
Wind gusts reached 87 mph at Nawiliwili and 84 mph at Lihue
facts.source_name: Maui Now (citing Hawaii congressional delegation letter)

facts.fact: A wind gust up to 92 mph was recorded at Puu Lua on Kauai
Rainfall in Kauai's higher elevations reached 17 inches
The highest measured rain total was just shy of 16 inches at Lower Limahuli, near Haena
Storm surge of 2-4 feet hit the south and west coasts of Kauai and Niihau
Kauai County officials reported no storm-related deaths on Kauai or Niihau; Fire Chief Mike Gibson said all people reported trapped or unaccounted for were located
At least one storm-related injury was reported on Kauai
As of Tuesday evening, Kauai County had logged 10 residential and 4 business damage claims, a count county officials said would grow
Red Cross opened five areas of refuge on Kauai, sheltering more than 300 people at the storm's peak; three overnight shelters remained open for residents who could not yet return home
Lihue Airport reopened at 11:15 a.m. Tuesday after closing ahead of the storm; it began operating on restored commercial power at 5 p.m. Thursday

Nawiliwili Harbor was reopened by the U.S. Coast Guard Captain of the Port before 5 p.m. Tuesday, but Port Allen remained closed to commercial operations as of Sept. 11 while divers restored navigational buoys
Lanai's only cargo harbor, Kaumalapau Harbor, was rendered inoperable, cutting off the main food and fuel supply route for the island's 3,300 residents, with an estimated two-week repair timeline
KIUC had restored 12 of its 15 transmission lines, with 72% of Kauai's power back on
About 100 outside utility personnel from Hawaiian Electric, Southern California Edison and HMS Construction were flown in via an Air Force C-17 Globemaster III to help KIUC crews

CPHC's final advisory on Lowell listed it as a post-tropical cyclone with max sustained winds of 50 mph, located about 815 miles northwest of Lihue and moving away from Hawaii; this was Advisory Number 60, the last one issued

Gov. Josh Green requested an expedited federal Major Disaster Declaration for Lowell; a presidential emergency declaration (a lesser, faster form of federal aid) had already been issued, covering emergency protective measures

Hawaii's congressional delegation (Sens. Schatz and Hirono, Reps. Case and Tokuda) sent a letter to the President on Sept. 9 urging approval of major disaster declarations for both Lowell and the earlier Hurricane Lala
All Kauai county, state and Department of Education offices and schools were closed through Friday, Sept. 11, along with county parks, campgrounds and the Wailua Golf Course

unknowns: No official total dollar damage estimate for Hurricane Lowell has been published yet (Hurricane Lala's $67M FEMA-eligible estimate took roughly a month to compile; Lowell's equivalent figure was not found in any source as of Sept 14).

No comprehensive, final count of damaged homes/structures on Kauai exists yet: county assessments and self-reported claims are still being compiled (early counts of 10 residential/4 business on Sept 8 do not reflect the fuller scope described later in coverage).
No breakdown of the injury total beyond 'at least one' — number injured, severity, and hospitalizations are not detailed in any source found.
No confirmed hard date for 100% power restoration; KIUC leadership (Bissell) says only that more clarity is expected 'in the next couple of days' as of Sept 14.
No exact headcount remains for how many people are still in the 3 open shelters as of Sept 13-14 (only the 300-person peak figure is given).

Whether President Trump has approved (vs. still reviewing) the Major Disaster Declaration request for Lowell is unconfirmed — as of the Sept 14 letter, the delegation was still 'urging approval,' meaning it had not yet been granted.
No confirmed reopening date for Port Allen commercial operations or Lanai's Kaumalapau Harbor beyond the initial ~2-week estimate given Sept 9.
No update found on whether Kauai's schools/county offices reopened after the initial Sept 11 closure date, or if closures were extended.
warnings: CONTRADICTION - do not attribute a death to Hurricane Lowell: A CNN headline ('At least 1 dead in Hawaii after Hurricane Lowell...', published 2026-09-06) surfaced in search but the article itself returned HTTP 451 and could not be opened directly to verify. Kauai County officials explicitly stated on 2026-09-08 (Kauai Now, Fire Chief Mike Gibson) that there were NO storm-related deaths on Kauai or Niihau from Lowell. Separately, Hurricane Lala — a distinct, earlier storm that hit Hawaii's Big Island in mid-August 2026 — did cause 1 confirmed death (per CNN, AP/WRAL, NBC, Aug 16 2026 reporting). The 'at least 1 dead' framing almost certainly belongs to Lala, not Lowell; using it for Lowell would be a wrong-attribution publish blocker. Recommend one more direct-source check before air.

STORM CATEGORY DISCREPANCY: Kauai Now (2026-09-08) describes Lowell as a 'Category 3 storm' at its closest approach, while NBC News, Washington Post, and other wire-level coverage describe it as Category 2 with sustained winds near 110 mph. CPHC's own advisory language (110 mph sustained at approach) supports Category 2. Treat Category 2 as authoritative; flag Category 3 references as likely inaccurate.

AGE OF FACTS: The storm's closest approach and initial damage/casualty facts (deaths, injury count, first damage claims, port/airport closures) are dated 2026-09-06 through 2026-09-09 — 5 to 8 days old as of today (2026-09-14). Power-restoration percentages and shelter counts are fresher (Sept 11-14) and should be used as the current-state numbers; older figures should only be used for the timeline/trend, not as 'current status.'

Two separate, similarly-named storms are in play this month: Hurricane Lowell (Kauai/Niihau, landfall-adjacent Sept 7-8) and Hurricane Lala (Big Island, mid-August). Federal disaster-declaration requests and disaster-relief equipment (e.g., the Southern California Edison trucks airlifted to Kauai) are being shared/cross-referenced between the two storms in official statements — scripts must not merge their damage/casualty/dollar figures.

The Hawaii Emergency Management Agency's own storm-update page (dod.hawaii.gov) contains no specific outage numbers, injury counts, or death tolls — it is thinner on hard numbers than the news-wire and county sources used here; treat HIEMA as a status/timeline source, not the numeric source of record.

The 'no deaths' confirmation is itself now 6 days old (Sept 8) with no found reconfirmation as of Sept 14 — recommend a fresh county/HIEMA check immediately before the video ships, in case a delayed storm-related fatality has since been confirmed.
